title: Climate-driven Modeling of the Initial Development of Brazilian Forest Species Under Current and Future Climates

authors.display_name: Maria Tereza Alves Martins de Faria

abstract: Abstract Modeling the initial development stage helps assess climate change impacts and species vulnerability under future scenarios. This study calibrated and validated two development models - the Phyllochron (Phyl) and Wang and Engel (WE) - under field conditions and identified potential alterations in the development of Brazilian forest species ( Bauhinia forficata , Ceiba speciosa , Handroanthus chrysotrichus , Handroanthus impetiginosus , and Tabebuia roseoalba ) throughout the 21st century. The Phyl and WE models estimate daily leaf appearance, which, when integrated over time, provides the duration of initial development. Field experiments conducted between 2022 and 2024 supported model calibration and validation. The best-performing model was applied to simulate development under current (1995–2014) and three future periods (2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100) and three socioeconomic scenarios (SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5). Sixteen General Circulation Models from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP-CMIP6) were used. Both models accurately estimated leaf number for all species, with lower precision for development duration. The Phyl model performed better for C. speciosa (RMSE = 1.30 leaves, 29.8 days) and H. chrysotrichus (1.41 leaves, 23.0 days), while the WE model performed better for B. forficata (1.14 leaves, 11.9 days), H. impetiginosus (1.50 leaves, 32.3 days), and T. roseoalba (1.32 leaves, 25.2 days). Projected temperature increases (+ 1.3 to + 4.5 °C) will alter leaf emergence and development duration, with reductions (− 1 to − 55 days) for sowing from February to July and increases (+ 1 to + 24 days) from August to January. Adjusting sowing schedules and controlling seedling environments are key adaptation strategies under global warming. Graphical Abstract
problem: Research on the developmental responses of Brazilian native forest species to climate change is limited, and existing models have not been validated for these species, hindering predictions of climate impacts and the design of effective adaptation measures.
method: This study calibrated and validated two development models, Phyllochron and Wang and Engel, using field data to project the initial development of five Brazilian forest species under future climate scenarios from sixteen general circulation models.
task: The task is to project alterations in the initial development of five Brazilian forest species under current and future climate scenarios by calibrating and validating two development models.
innovation: This study calibrates and applies two development models to project the impacts of future climate scenarios on the initial leaf development duration of five native Brazilian forest species, revealing species-specific responses and key adaptation strategies such as adjusting sowing schedules.

Daily mean air temperature (Tmean) data from 16 NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 GCMs (Table S2) was extracted for the grid point nearest to Itajubá and used as input in the temperature functions, i.e., TTd (Phyl) or [f(T)] (WE) (Fig. 3). This climate models are provided by the Climate Analytics Group and NASA Ames Research Center, and made available through the NASA Center for Climate Simulation (NCCS) portal (Thrasher et al. 2022) at <https://www.nccs.nasa.gov /services/data-collections/land-based-products/nex-gddp% 3E and have a horizontal resolution of 0.25° (latitude/long itude), suitable for local-scale studies.

The General Circulation Models (GCMs) from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP-CMIP6) dataset are derived from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), representing a new generation of climate models with high spatial resolution due to bias correction (Thrasher et al. 2022). i.e., the NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 models are capable of projecting air temperature at a finer scale, making them suitable for assessing local climate trends (Dias et al. 2024; Fagundes et al. 2025a, b), as intended in this study.
